title: Conflicts and reconciliation
summary: What to do with the wounds, bitterness and conflicts between people. How to understand forgiveness (which is not pretending nothing happened), how to resolve disputes God's way, and how not to let anger turn into bitterness.

sections.heading: The wound and bitterness: what happens inside me

items.comment: Paul calls things by their name: bitterness, wrath, clamor, anger. A hurt left unworked does not disappear - it ferments and poisons us from within.

questions.text: Which of these "forms" of woundedness do you recognize in yourself today? Toward whom?

items.comment: A "root of bitterness" grows in hiding and "defiles many." Bitterness does not only hurt the one who did wrong - it first wounds the one who carries it.

questions.text: Who is most harmed by the bitterness you carry inside? How long have you been "watering" it?

items.comment: God warns Cain: "sin is crouching at the door, and it desires you, but you must rule over it." Unexpressed anger and envy, when fed, end in violence.

questions.text: Where in your relationships is "sin crouching at your door" - a grievance building that you have not yet crossed over into?

items.label: Cain: a warning turned into the first conflict
items.content: The words to Cain are a classic example of a "rule of action": God does not condemn the impulse of anger but calls us to master it before it grows. This is the first human relationship after the fall - and the first deadly conflict - shown within the frame of the great controversy: anger that is not dealt with becomes the field on which sin "crouches" and takes control. A grievance is not neutral; either you rule over it, or it begins to rule over you.

questions.text: What does it concretely mean for you to "rule" over anger before the "sin crouching at the door" takes the initiative?

sections.heading: Anger: an emotion that need not sin

items.comment: "Be angry and do not sin" - anger in itself is not a sin, but when we store it up, we give "a place to the devil." The point is not to keep it overnight.

questions.text: How is experiencing anger different from "living" in it? What do you usually do with your anger?

items.label: "do not let the sun go down on your anger"
items.content: Paul does not demand that anger vanish instantly, but he sets it a short shelf life: until sunset. In this view, forgiveness is a conscious "setting aside of the grievance" - a decision, not the spontaneous fading of a feeling. The boundary "by nightfall" guards against a momentary anger having time to take root as bitterness and to harden from an emotion into an attitude. Anger that is not dealt with in time is exactly the place Paul calls a "place for the devil."

questions.text: What might be "your sunset" - a specific moment in the day or week - that could become the time to settle accounts with anger before it hardens?

items.comment: "Quick to listen, slow to anger" - because "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God." Hasty anger rarely leads to good, even though it feels justified.

questions.text: In which situations are you "quick to speak, slow to listen"? How does that change the course of a conflict?

items.comment: "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger." In a conflict it is not only the content but also the tone that decides whether we move toward escalation or toward reconciliation.

questions.text: Recall your last argument - what would one "gentle tone" have changed in it instead of a sharp word?

sections.heading: Forgiveness at its source: because I have been forgiven

items.comment: "Forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you." The measure and the power of my forgiveness is first of all how much I myself have been given.

questions.text: Is it easier for you to believe that God has forgiven you, or that you must forgive others? How are these two things connected?

items.label: "to forgive" / ἀφίημι (aphiēmi) - to release a debt
items.content: The most common New Testament verb for "to forgive" is *aphiēmi* - literally "to let go, release, send away." The same word is used for cancelling a debt (Matt 18:27, 32) and for the forgiveness of sins in the Lord's Prayer (Matt 6:12). The image is very concrete: to forgive is to let go of the certificate of debt by which you could hold someone. You do not deny that the debt existed - you consciously give up the right to collect it.

questions.text: What are you holding in your hand as a "certificate of debt" against someone? What would it mean to let it go without pretending the debt never existed?

items.comment: "Bearing with one another and forgiving each other" - forgiveness is a decision and a process within a community, not a one-time feeling.

questions.text: Toward whom do you have "something against" today? What would it practically mean to begin the process of forgiving that person?

items.label: "to forgive" / χαρίζομαι (charizomai) (Ef 4,32; Kol 3,13)
items.content: In Eph 4:32 and Col 3:13 Paul does not use the ordinary word for "to cancel debts" but *charizomai* - a verb related to *charis* ("grace"). To forgive is therefore to "give grace" in the way God has given to us in Christ. It is not erasing the fact of the wrong but giving up the right to revenge and showing the guilty person undeserved kindness.

questions.text: If forgiveness is "a gift of grace," what sets it apart from pretending the wrong never happened?

items.comment: Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough; Jesus answers: "seventy-seven times" - meaning forgiveness is not a limit but a steady attitude.

questions.text: What makes it easier to count wrongs than to release them? Where does your "patience for forgiving" end?

items.label: "seventy-seven times" and Lamech (Mt 18,22; Rdz 4,24)
items.content: Jesus' "seventy-seven times" (it can also be translated "seventy times seven") is a deliberate reversal of Lamech's words in Gen 4:24, who boasted of vengeance "seventy-seven times." Where a culture of sin multiplies revenge without limit, the kingdom of God multiplies forgiveness without limit. This is a deliberate change in the logic of relationships within the great controversy: from the escalation of revenge to the escalation of grace.

questions.text: Where in your relationships does the "logic of Lamech" (revenge) operate, and where could you introduce the "logic of Jesus" (forgiveness without counting)?

items.comment: The parable of the unforgiving servant: someone forgiven an enormous debt throttles a fellow servant over a trifle. Not forgiving others is forgetting how much we ourselves have received.

questions.text: When you think of a wrong you find hard to forgive, set beside it the debt God has forgiven you - how does that comparison look?

items.label: What forgiveness is NOT
items.content: It is worth clarifying forgiveness by saying what it is not. To forgive is not the same as to excuse ("nothing happened"), to explain away the wrong by circumstances, or to pretend there was no fault. Forgiveness actually confirms that a wrong took place - and yet it consciously releases the guilty person from the debt and opens the way to repairing the relationship. That is why true pardon is not weakness toward evil but the strongest response to it: it names evil as evil while breaking its power over us.

questions.text: Which counterfeit of forgiveness do you sometimes mistake for forgiveness: excusing, explaining away, or pretending?

items.comment: "When you stand praying, forgive." Jesus links prayer with a readiness to forgive - a grievance we hold blocks our relationship not only with a person but also with God.

questions.text: Is there a person whose face comes back to you during prayer? What would it mean to "forgive" them right there?

sections.heading: Conflict: how to talk and seek peace

items.comment: "If your brother sins, go and tell him his fault between the two of you alone." The first step is neither gossip nor silence but a direct, discreet conversation with the person concerned.

questions.text: How do you usually react to being hurt: stay silent, tell others, or go to the person? What would the step of going "one to one" change?

items.comment: If the conversation does not help, only then are witnesses brought in, and finally the community. The goal is not to "win" but to win back a brother - escalation is a last resort, not the first move.

questions.text: What does it say about the goal of this procedure that it begins with the smallest possible circle of people?

items.label: Mt 18,15-17 in the context of care for a brother, not a criminal trial
items.content: The procedure in Matt 18:15-17 is placed right after the parable of the lost sheep (Matt 18:12-14) and just before the teaching on forgiveness (vv. 21-35). This is a pastoral context: the goal of the successive steps is not disciplinary or "evidentiary" but the recovery of a person. The gradual involvement of witnesses and the community is meant to protect the dignity of both the wounded and the one in error, not to publicly shame them.

questions.text: How does the use of this procedure change when its goal is to "win the brother" rather than to "prove him guilty"?

items.comment: "If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone." Peace is my task "so far as it depends on me" - the other person will not always take the hand I hold out.

questions.text: Where does "your part" in reconciliation end? What do you do when you have done your part and the other side does not respond?

items.label: Paul's two qualifications: the realism of peace
items.content: Paul hedges the command of peace with two conditions: "if possible" and "so far as it depends on you." This is sober realism - reconciliation requires two parties, and you answer only for your own. The distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation is key here: you can forgive (let go of the grievance before God) unilaterally and always; you can be reconciled (rebuild the relationship) only when the other side also wants it, sometimes confesses and makes amends. Doing "your part" is not a failure, even if the other side stays silent.

questions.text: Where do you confuse "reconciliation did not work out" with "I have not forgiven"? What changes when you separate these two things?

items.comment: Jesus tells us to interrupt even an offering in order to first reconcile with a brother. Repairing the relationship comes before the religious act - worship does not replace reconciliation.

questions.text: Is there a relationship you keep "putting off" while God seems to be saying: first go and be reconciled? What is holding you back?

items.comment: "Do not repay evil for evil... overcome evil with good." Giving up revenge is not weakness - it is handing justice over to God and breaking the spiral of retaliation.

questions.text: Which is harder for you: not striking back, or actively responding with good? Why?

application.text: Wounds in relationships are unavoidable, but bitterness is not. God does not ask you to pretend the wrong never happened; he invites you - just as you yourself have been given forgiveness in Christ - to stop holding the debt and to seek reconciliation. Anger need not become sin, and conflict need not end in a broken bond, if we walk God's way: directly, gently, and at peace so far as it depends on us.
application.challenge: Think of one person toward whom you carry a grievance. First, in prayer, "forgive" them before God - hand him the right to justice (Rom 12:19). Then, if it is possible and safe, take one step toward reconciliation "one to one" this week (Mt 18:15): a conversation, a message, a gesture. Write down what was holding you back and what changed once you made a move.
